questions.prompt: When does a Swift macro expand and generate new code?

options.text: At compile time before the binary is linked.
options.explanation: Right. Swift expands macros during compilation and type-checks the generated code.

options.text: At app launch before the first screen loads.
options.explanation: Wrong. Macros finish expanding before your app binary is built.

options.text: At runtime using Objective-C message forwarding.
options.explanation: Wrong. Swift macros do not rely on runtime forwarding or Objective-C.

options.text: Inside the linker after object files finish.
options.explanation: Wrong. Expansion happens earlier while compiling syntax trees.

questions.prompt: What symbol always starts a freestanding macro call in Swift?

options.text: The dollar sign ($).
options.explanation: Wrong. The dollar sign accesses a property wrapper projected value.

options.text: The hash symbol (#).
options.explanation: Right. Freestanding macros like #Predicate and #line always start with #.

options.text: The at symbol (@).
options.explanation: Wrong. The at symbol is used for attached macros and attributes.

options.text: The tilde symbol (~).
options.explanation: Wrong. The tilde is for noncopyable types like ~Copyable, not macros.

questions.prompt: What symbol always starts an attached macro in Swift?

options.text: The hash symbol (#).
options.explanation: Wrong. The hash symbol is for freestanding macros.

options.text: The underscore (_).
options.explanation: Wrong. Underscores are for backing storage names or omitted labels.

options.text: The at symbol (@).
options.explanation: Right. Attached macros like @Observable sit before a declaration with @.

options.text: The question mark (?).
options.explanation: Wrong. A question mark marks an optional type or optional chaining.

questions.prompt: Which library do Swift macro plugins use to read and build syntax trees?

options.text: SwiftUI
options.explanation: Wrong. SwiftUI is a user interface framework, not a syntax parser.

options.text: Foundation
options.explanation: Wrong. Foundation provides base types and utilities, not compiler AST tools.

options.text: Combine
options.explanation: Wrong. Combine handles reactive event streams over time.

options.text: SwiftSyntax
options.explanation: Right. Macro compiler plugins import SwiftSyntax to inspect and emit syntax nodes.

questions.prompt: How do Swift macros differ from C preprocessor macros?

options.text: Swift macros transform parsed syntax trees and are type-checked.
options.explanation: Right. Swift checks types before and after expansion on structured syntax trees.

options.text: Swift macros paste raw text lines before the parser runs.
options.explanation: Wrong. That describes C preprocessor macros, not Swift macros.

options.text: Swift macros can skip type checks for faster builds.
options.explanation: Wrong. The compiler always type-checks the expanded Swift code.

options.text: Swift macros only work in C header bridging files.
options.explanation: Wrong. Swift macros are native Swift plugins used in Swift files.

questions.prompt: Which two roles belong to freestanding macros?

options.text: Member and peer
options.explanation: Wrong. Member and peer are attached macro roles.

options.text: Expression and declaration
options.explanation: Right. Freestanding macros use @freestanding(expression) or @freestanding(declaration).

options.text: Accessor and extension
options.explanation: Wrong. Accessor and extension are attached macro roles.

options.text: Body and memberAttribute
options.explanation: Wrong. Body and memberAttribute are attached macro roles.

questions.prompt: Why does Swift run macro plugins inside a sandbox?

options.text: To allow macros to upload crash logs during builds.
options.explanation: Wrong. The sandbox blocks network access completely.

options.text: To let macros edit files anywhere on your Mac.
options.explanation: Wrong. The sandbox blocks filesystem reads and writes.

options.text: To keep builds safe and repeatable with no disk or network access.
options.explanation: Right. Because plugins see only the macro syntax node, builds stay safe and repeatable.

options.text: To disable Swift 6 concurrency checks inside packages.
options.explanation: Wrong. The sandbox isolates plugin execution and has nothing to do with concurrency settings.

questions.prompt: Which attached macro role adds new methods or properties inside a struct or class?

options.text: @attached(peer)
options.explanation: Wrong. Peer adds sibling declarations alongside the target in the same scope.

options.text: @attached(accessor)
options.explanation: Wrong. Accessor adds getters, setters, or observers to a property.

options.text: @attached(body)
options.explanation: Wrong. Body generates or wraps a function or accessor body.

options.text: @attached(member)
options.explanation: Right. The member role generates new declarations inside the attached type.

questions.prompt: What does `@attached(memberAttribute)` do when placed on a type?

options.text: It applies attributes to declarations inside that type.
options.explanation: Right. For example, @Observable uses memberAttribute to attach @ObservationTracked to stored properties.

options.text: It deletes private stored properties from the type.
options.explanation: Wrong. Swift macros are additive and cannot delete existing declarations.

options.text: It converts a class into a value-type struct.
options.explanation: Wrong. Macros cannot change a declaration's kind from class to struct.

options.text: It creates a free global function outside the type.
options.explanation: Wrong. Global or sibling declarations come from peer or freestanding macros.

questions.prompt: Which role adds an async overload next to a completion-handler method in the same scope?

options.text: @attached(accessor)
options.explanation: Wrong. Accessor adds property getters, setters, or observers.

options.text: @attached(peer)
options.explanation: Right. Peer macros add new declarations alongside the target declaration.

options.text: @attached(extension)
options.explanation: Wrong. Extension macros add a separate extension block for a type.

options.text: @freestanding(expression)
options.explanation: Wrong. Freestanding expression macros evaluate to a value at a call site.

questions.prompt: How does a modern attached macro add protocol conformances to a type?

options.text: With `@attached(member)` only.
options.explanation: Wrong. Member adds properties or methods inside the type, not protocol conformances.

options.text: With `@attached(peer)`.
options.explanation: Wrong. Peer adds sibling declarations in the same scope.

options.text: With `@attached(extension, conformances: ...)`.
options.explanation: Right. The extension role with a conformances list adds extensions and protocol conformances.

options.text: With `@freestanding(declaration)`.
options.explanation: Wrong. Freestanding declaration macros are not attached to a type.

questions.prompt: Why do macro declarations include a `names:` list like `names: named(init)`?

options.text: To rename user-written properties before parsing starts.
options.explanation: Wrong. Macros cannot delete or rename declarations you already wrote.

options.text: To skip running the plugin during release builds.
options.explanation: Wrong. The compiler always runs macro expansion when building code.

options.text: To export symbols directly into Objective-C headers.
options.explanation: Wrong. Name specifiers are for Swift compiler name lookup.

options.text: To tell the compiler what symbol names the macro may generate.
options.explanation: Right. The compiler uses name specifiers for symbol lookup before running the plugin.

questions.prompt: What does `@ObservationIgnored` do inside an `@Observable` class?

options.text: It skips observation tracking for that stored property.
options.explanation: Right. Changes to an @ObservationIgnored property do not trigger observation updates.

options.text: It removes the property from memory during release builds.
options.explanation: Wrong. The property still exists and stores values normally.

options.text: It makes the property thread-safe across actors.
options.explanation: Wrong. @ObservationIgnored only turns off observation tracking.

options.text: It turns a stored property into a property wrapper.
options.explanation: Wrong. It is a macro-recognized marker, not a property wrapper.

questions.prompt: Which statement about `@attached(body)` macros is true?

options.text: You can attach up to five body macros to one function.
options.explanation: Wrong. At most one body macro can be attached to a function.

options.text: It can generate or wrap the body of a function or accessor.
options.explanation: Right. `@attached(body)` produces or wraps the body of a function or accessor.

options.text: It adds a new protocol conformance to a class.
options.explanation: Wrong. Extension macros add protocol conformances.

options.text: It only works with freestanding `#` syntax.
options.explanation: Wrong. Body is an attached macro role.

questions.prompt: What is the main build-graph downside of adding custom Swift macros to an app?

options.text: Every screen must switch from SwiftUI to UIKit.
options.explanation: Wrong. Macros work independently of UI frameworks.

options.text: Generated code skips Swift 6 data-race checks.
options.explanation: Wrong. Expanded code goes through normal Swift 6 type and concurrency checks.

options.text: Macro targets depend on SwiftSyntax and lengthen clean build times.
options.explanation: Right. Compiling SwiftSyntax and running plugin binaries adds measurable build overhead.

options.text: Apps using macros cannot ship on the App Store.
options.explanation: Wrong. Macro plugins run at compile time and do not ship inside the app binary.

questions.prompt: Why can Swift macros replace property wrappers in cases like `@Observable`?

options.text: Macros run in the cloud instead of on the developer's Mac.
options.explanation: Wrong. Macro plugins run locally inside a sandbox during compilation.

options.text: Property wrappers cannot store Int or String values.
options.explanation: Wrong. Property wrappers store any value type or reference type.

options.text: Property wrappers cannot compile under Swift 6 mode.
options.explanation: Wrong. Property wrappers work normally in Swift 6.

options.text: Macros work across a whole type without creating per-property wrapper structs.
options.explanation: Right. Macros add accessors, tracking storage, and protocol conformance without extra wrapper objects.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain how freestanding macros and attached macros differ in syntax and purpose, and give one example of each.

rubric.criterion: States that freestanding macros start with # and stand alone without attaching to a declaration
States that attached macros start with @ and modify or expand the declaration they are placed on
Gives one example of each (such as #Predicate or #line, and @Observable)

questions.modelAnswer: Freestanding macros start with a hash symbol (#) and stand on their own to produce a value or declaration, like #Predicate or #Preview. Attached macros start with an at symbol (@) and sit right before a declaration to add code to it, like @Observable on a class.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain why Swift macros are safer than C preprocessor macros and what the sandbox enforces.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Swift macros transform structured syntax trees (ASTs) rather than pasting raw text
States that the compiler type-checks the macro inputs and the expanded Swift code
States that the compiler plugin sandbox blocks file disk access and network access

questions.modelAnswer: Unlike C preprocessor macros that paste raw text, Swift macros work on structured syntax trees using SwiftSyntax. The compiler checks types before and after expansion, so bad generated code fails at build time. Macro plugins also run in a sandbox with no disk or network access, keeping builds safe and repeatable.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain how `@Observable` works by combining multiple attached macro roles.

rubric.criterion: Explains that @Observable adds tracking storage inside the class using the member role
Explains that it applies @ObservationTracked to stored properties using memberAttribute
Explains that it adds Observable protocol conformance using the extension role

questions.modelAnswer: @Observable combines three attached macro roles on a class. It uses the member role to add tracking storage inside the class. It uses memberAttribute to attach @ObservationTracked to stored properties. Finally, it uses the extension role to add Observable protocol conformance.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, compare Swift macros and property wrappers on where they apply, runtime storage, and build cost.

rubric.criterion: States that property wrappers apply only to stored properties and create backing wrapper storage like _prop
States that macros work on expressions, functions, types, and properties at compile time without backing wrapper objects
Notes the build cost trade-off that macros require SwiftSyntax

questions.modelAnswer: Property wrappers apply only to stored properties and create a backing wrapper instance like _score at runtime. Swift macros rewrite syntax trees at compile time with no per-property wrapper object. Macros also work on expressions, functions, and whole types. However, custom macros add a SwiftSyntax dependency that slows down clean builds.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain when a senior or staff engineer should avoid writing a custom macro and what debugging tool Xcode provides.

rubric.criterion: Explains that teams should prefer generics, protocol extensions, or property wrappers when they can express the logic
Mentions build-time cost from SwiftSyntax or harder readability/control flow
Names Expand Macro in Xcode as the tool to inspect generated code

questions.modelAnswer: Avoid custom macros when generics, protocol extensions, or property wrappers already solve the problem cleanly. Macros add SwiftSyntax to your build graph, slow down clean builds, and hide generated code from plain reading. When you do use a macro, you can inspect what it generates using Expand Macro in Xcode.
